# Development and Validation of a Novel Deep Learning Model to Predict Pharmacologic Closure of Patent Ductus Arteriosus in Premature Infants

**Authors:** Puneet Sharma; Addison Gearhart; Guangze Luo; Anil Palepu; Cindy Wang; Joshua Mayourian; Kristyn Beam; Fotios Spyropoulos; Andrew J. Powell; Philip Levy; Andrew Beam

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Neonatology, Emory University School of Medicine | 2Department of Cardiology, Boston Children’s Hospital | 3Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health | 4Department of Health Sciences & Technology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology | 5Department of Statistics, Harvard University | 6Department of Neonatology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center | 7Division of Newborn Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital | 8Division of Newborn Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital

## Abstract

The patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is associated with significant morbidity and mortality in the preterm infant. While pharmacotherapy can be effective, it is difficult to predict whether a patient will respond, leading to delays in care. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool to interpret clinical data to predict clinical outcomes but has not yet been applied to this question. We aimed to train and validate a novel deep learning model to predict the likelihood of PDA closure after an initial course of pharmacotherapy in preterm infants.

We identified a retrospective cohort of 174 preterm infants who received pharmacologic treatment for their PDA. After collecting relevant perinatal data and pre-treatment echocardiograms, we randomized the subjects into training and validation sets in a 70:30 split. We trained two distinct convolutional neural networks (CNN), one based on echocardiograms alone and the other on both echocardiograms and perinatal data. We compared the performance of the CNNs against controls of random forest and logistic regression models trained on perinatal data alone.

The rate of PDA closure after initial course of pharmacotherapy was 60% in our cohort. The 174 echocardiograms collected for all subjects included 1926 clips. We successfully randomized 121 infants (1387 clips) into the training set and 53 (539 clips) into the validation set. The multimodal CNN had an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.82, outperforming the imaging-only model (AUC = 0.66). Additionally, the multimodal CNN outperformed logistic regression (AUC = 0.66) and random forest (AUC = 0.74) models.

Our novel, multimodal CNN shows promise for clinicians who do not currently have a reliable tool to predict success of PDA closure after initial course of pharmacotherapy. This investigation represents the first attempt to utilize deep learning methodology to predict this outcome.

## Introduction

The patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a major focus of neonatal intensive care due to its risk of mortality and association with several major morbidities such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), necrotizing enterocolitis, pulmonary hemorrhage, intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), acute kidney injury, and pulmonary hypertension (1–4). Given this risk profile, many clinicians seek to treat the PDA despite inconsistent evidence that treatment improves long-term outcomes (5–7). The most definitive way to close the PDA is through either surgical ligation or transcatheter device occlusion. Still, many clinicians elect to pursue pharmacologic closure first as it is non-invasive and typically effective (6–7). The most common pharmacologic agents used are acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and indomethacin which have a success rate between 60–70% within a week from initiation (7).

Despite the success rate of pharmacotherapy, the best approach for the infants that do not respond to an initial course remains to be determined (8–10). Some centers elect for additional courses of pharmacotherapy. This approach may improve closure rates; however, it carries an increased risk of serious morbidities, such as periventricular leukomalacia or BPD (8,10). Other centers pursue procedural closure after an unsuccessful course of pharmacotherapy. This practice has certainly increased with the proliferation of transcatheter device occlusion, but it is complicated by the fact that many neonates are cared for in centers that do not offer procedural closure (11–13). Furthermore, transporting an infant for procedural closure carries some risk and can often be delayed by insurance providers and/or medical instability. Altogether, clinicians are left with uncertainty in the management of these infants as both delayed closure and repeat pharmacotherapy are associated with increased morbidity (1–4, 8, 10). Prior studies have attempted to identify serum biomarkers predictive of successful closure, but results have been inconsistent (14–16). While there is evidence that echocardiographic parameters can predict spontaneous PDA closure, it has not been studied in patients receiving pharmacologic therapy (17).

Machine learning, particularly deep learning, is a discipline of computer science that has emerged as a powerful methodology for prediction modeling (18,19). It is well-suited for medical imaging data given its ability to extract and interpret complex data (20). One specific area of promise is the interpretation of echocardiogram data as recent models have been developed to predict ejection fraction, recognize signs of volume overload, and detect the presence of a PDA from echocardiogram data alone (21–23). Despite this potential, there has yet to be a study using deep learning to predict the response of the PDA to pharmacologic treatment through analysis of echocardiogram images. As such, the objective of this study was to train and validate a novel deep learning model to predict the likelihood of PDA closure after an initial course of pharmacotherapy in preterm infants.

## Methods

### Defining the Cohort:

We performed a retrospective cohort study of all preterm infants (delivered at less than 37 weeks of gestational age) who received pharmacologic treatment of a PDA at the neonatal intensive care units of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) and Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH) in Boston, Massachusetts between January 2016 and December 2021. This cohort was identified by querying the Vermont Oxford Network (VON) for neonates admitted to these units during our enrollment period. VON is a nonprofit, collaborative effort of health care professionals dedicated to improving the quality, safety and value of neonatal care through data-driven quality improvement, education, and research (24). BIDMC and BWH submit standardized, structured data to VON on all patients admitted to their units. Infants were identified from VON if they have one of the following diagnoses: “acetamin,” “ibuprofen,” “indometh,” “PDA,” or “PDAsurg.” The presence of a PDA was then confirmed for each enrolled infant by reviewing the pre-treatment echocardiogram. Infants were excluded if they received indomethacin for IVH prophylaxis, had early termination of therapy, did not have a pre-treatment echocardiogram, or had other cardiac lesions. For purposes of this study, a pre-treatment echocardiogram was defined as an echocardiogram obtained no more than 24 hours prior to initiation of pharmacotherapy. The requirement for informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Boards at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and Boston Children’s Hospital. The study was performed in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

For each subject, we determined whether the patient has successful closure after the initial course of pharmacotherapy. Success was defined as no evidence of repeat courses of pharmacotherapy, transcatheter occlusion, or surgical ligation prior to NICU discharge. This clinically oriented definition of success was used instead of anatomic confirmation on echocardiogram as it was not routine practice during the enrollment period to obtain a post-treatment echocardiogram. For infants that did have a post-treatment echocardiogram, the images were not reviewed to minimize potential bias against those who did not. This would have made it difficult to classify a patient who may have anatomic of evidence of a persistent PDA but otherwise had symptomatic improvement where no further treatment was pursued by the clinician. The definition of a single treatment course was identical at both sites and specific to the medication being used. For indomethacin, this was three parenteral doses every 12 hours at either 0.2 or 0.3 mg/kg depending on chronologic age, and for acetaminophen, it was 15 mg/kg every 6 hours for a minimum of three days, although the clinician was allowed to extend to a total duration of seven days pending clinical response. The choice of medication and the route of administration (parenteral or enteral) of acetaminophen was per clinician discretion.

We obtained the pre-treatment echocardiogram for all enrolled infants. All studies were obtained in-unit without procedural anesthesia on a Philips ultrasound machine. For infants that had multiple echocardiograms prior to initiation of pharmacotherapy, we selected the echocardiogram collected closest to the date of initiation. If the study file could not be located, the corresponding patient was excluded from the cohort. For each study, a cardiologist specialized in imaging (AG) blinded to success of treatment reviewed images and classified them into specific view types relevant to the PDA (Table 1). If a study did not have any clips with the predetermined views of interest, it was excluded from the cohort. In addition to the pre-treatment echocardiograms, relevant perinatal data was collected on the remaining cohort (Supplemental Table 1). The cohort was then randomized into training and validation sets in a 70:30 split.

### Model Training and Validation:

To fit the 3D computer vision model necessary to achieve the objective of the study, we first had to convert the echocardiogram to mp4 format. We then performed a list of data preprocessing steps including center cropping, resize and standardization. First, we center-cropped the video so that each frame is in the dimension of 512 × 512 pixels. We then re-sized the images to be 128 × 128 to strike a balance between image resolution and demand on computational resources. Previous literature has shown resolutions ranging from 128–400 pixels with adequate performance (21, 25–27). Finally, we applied z-score normalization to each video to accelerate training by enhancing gradient descent convergence and minimizing numerical instability. This technique standardizes the data by adjusting its mean to 0 and its standard deviation to 1, ensuring comparability across video features and eliminating biases caused by differing distributions.

Three distinct convolutional neural networks (CNN), each using a distinct architecture, were trained on the imaging data only of the training set. These architectures included a scratch build of a 3D CNN and two transfer learning approaches with pre-trained based models of Swin3D and EchoNet-Pediatric (28–30). Swin3D is a three-dimensional version of Swin Transformer, which is widely used for 3D object detection and segmentation (29). EchoNet-Pediatric is a deep learning model developed to assess ventricular function and predict ejection fraction (30). For all three models, an adaptive moment estimation (ADAM) optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.0001 was chosen. The ADAM optimizer stabilizes model updates by using an exponentially decaying moving average of past gradients. Additionally, it adjusts the learning rate for each parameter dynamically during training, ensuring efficient and adaptive optimization. Binary Cross Entropy Loss was used for this binary classification task to measure the difference between the predicted probability and the true binary label, penalizing incorrect predictions more heavily as they deviate from the true label. The final fully connected layer was replaced with an identity layer. The performance of these architectures was then assessed on the validation set to determine which was most successful as defined by AUC. After selecting the best architecture, we then compared the performance of this imaging only CNN to a multimodal model trained on both echocardiogram clips and the perinatal factors described in Supplemental Table 1. For this multimodal model, the perinatal factors were concatenated with the classifier head and then fed into the output layer. For both models, we validated on subsets of the entire cohort that were stratified by domain type present in the study (Table 1). We then compared the performance of the computer vision model against control predictive models, namely logistic regression and random forest trained on the perinatal factors only.

To assess the interpretability of the computer vision model, we generated saliency maps for all clips included in the model. The saliency map highlights regions of a given input image that are important for producing the prediction on that image. We also had the clips that the model had the highest confidence in prediction and lowest confidence reviewed by a cardiologist specializing in imaging (AG) to assess the image quality of the study.

## Results

### Study Population:

We identified 465 premature infants (182 from BIDMC and 283 from BWH) who met inclusion criteria for the study. From this population, 250 met our exclusion criteria and therefore were removed from the cohort. Of the remaining 215 infants, 41 were removed from the cohort due to concerns with their pre-treatment echocardiograms. Our final cohort included 174 infants of which 104 (60%) were from BIDMC and 70 (40%) from BWH. Figure 1 provides further details on the enrollment process, including details on the excluded patients.

Of the 174 infants, 105 (60%) had successful closure after the initial course of pharmacotherapy. The median gestational age at birth of the cohort was 26.1 weeks, with only 20 infants (11%) born at a gestational age greater than 28 weeks. While there was no statistically significant difference in the median age at treatment between the birth hospitals (5 days at BIDMC v 4 days at BWH, p = 0.29), there was a difference in pharmacologic agents most used. Indomethacin was used in 66% of patients at BIDMC and only 39% at BWH (p = 0.01). Additionally, infants born at BWH were more likely to have successful closure (70% v 54%, p = 0.05). The infants from BWH were also of a greater birth weight (883 g v 760 g, p = 0.01) and gestational age (27.0 v 25.3, p = 0.01) than those from BIDMC. There were no other notable differences between the infants born at the two hospitals (Supplemental Table 2). After randomization, a total of 121 (70%) infants were included in the training set while 53 (30%) infants were allocated to the validation set. There were no significant differences between the two sets (Table 2).

### Echocardiogram Labeling:

A total of 1926 clips comprised the 174 echocardiograms of the enrolled patients; 1156 (60%) of the clips were from BIDMC patients and 770 (40%) were from BWH, which reflects the overall proportion of patients in the cohort. After randomization, the training set included 1387 (72%) clips and the validation set included 539 (28%) clips, which reflects the intended 70/30 patient split between the two sets with no overlap. While the median clips per study was similar between the training and validation sets, the interquartile range for both sets was rather large suggesting a great deal of variance in study length from one patient to another (Table 2). This variance was also reflected in views included in each study as well, with most clips from the “non-PDA” domain (43%). Also of note, not every domain was included in each study, the most common domain was “non-PDA,” which was included in 149 studies (86%). Table 1 provides a detailed summary of the composition of studies by domain.

### Model Performance:

Of the three architectures, EchoNet-Pediatric achieved the greatest AUC on the imaging only computer vision model and as such was selected framework for the study (Supplemental Table 3).

For the imaging-only model, the overall AUC for predicting successful closure on the validation set was 0.66, with similar performance in the subgroups stratified by domain type. However, with addition of the collected perinatal data to the model, the overall performance of the computer vision model improved to 0.82 with similarly consistent improvement across all domains (Central Illustration). While the imaging-only model performed at the level of logistic regression, the imaging plus perinatal data model outperformed all other models including the random forest. The results of all models are summarized in Table 3.

Given that the multimodal CNN had the greatest AUC, we conducted further analyses to assess its performance. Figure 2 presents the model’s receiver operating characteristic curves. We compared its performance on the validation set and training set and found similar AUCs, suggesting it did not suffer from overfitting (Supplemental Table 4). Other measures of performance, such as F1 score, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value, are summarized in Table 4. Additionally, we queried the multimodal CNN to identify the clips for which it was most and least confident in its prediction. A cardiac imaging expert (AG) reviewed these clips for study quality, and her impressions are included in Supplemental Table 5. Finally, we generated saliency maps for the best and poorest performing clips, which are shown in Figure 3.

## Discussion

With this multicenter cohort, we developed a 3D computer vision model that predicted successful pharmacologic closure of the PDA after initial course with an AUC of 0.82. The model, which was developed via transfer learning on a EchoNet-Pediatric backbone, was based on pre-treatment echocardiogram and a select set of clinical variables. The addition of these clinical variables to the CNN improved the AUC from 0.66 to 0.82. This combined model outperformed our control logistic regression (AUC = 0.66) and random forest (AUC = 0.74) models trained on the clinical variables alone.

Management of the PDA in the neonatal intensive care setting remains a highly debated and complex area. Many clinicians struggle with the decision to treat the PDA as there is inconsistent evidence as to whether treatment improves the risk of morbidity (5–7). As such, the decision to treat is often made based on features in the echocardiogram that suggest hemodynamic significance (31). Due to minimal side effect profile and relative effectiveness, most clinicians initially elect for pharmacologic closure, but not every patient responds. Without a reliable way to identify whether a patient will respond, our model shows great promise in filling this gap in clinical practice. With just a pre-treatment echocardiogram and some readily available clinical parameters, clinicians can have more confidence in whether a patient will respond to pharmacotherapy before it is even initiated. This will allow for less delays in definitive closure by allowing the clinician to anticipate next steps, whether that be referral for procedural closure or repeat courses of pharmacotherapy.

Our work contributes to the growing body of literature on leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) to investigate the PDA. Multiple AI models have been developed to diagnose the PDA, but none of these approaches provide actionable information regarding treatment (22–23, 32–33). As such, our study represents a distinct utilization of deep learning to address this significant clinical need. The performance of our model compares favorably to studies that have employed traditional methods such as regression to predict closure (34–35). These regression models, however, still require manual interpretation of echocardiogram data by a trained physician. This limits their application in resource-scarce settings when compared to our model that does not require any interpretation separate from the AI. In addition to our model’s strong AUC, another promising metric of its performance is its F1 score (0.78). This demonstrates that the model has a good balance between precision and recall, which is crucial in a task such as predicting successful closure. That is not to say, however, that the model is without weaknesses. The biggest concern with its performance is its low specificity (0.70) and negative predictive value (0.66). These results suggest that a clinician using the model can be more confident that the PDA will respond when predicted but should continue to have some skepticism if the model suggests treatment will not be successful. While not perfect, the information provided by the model still provides the clinician with useful information with which to counsel families and inform decisions around referral.

As noted previously, a major strength of our study is its unique methodology, which includes training the model on a multicenter cohort with adequate randomization between training and validation sets. However, this strength needs to be interpreted within the framework of its limitations. One such limitation is that the model was internally validated. While this is a common approach in clinical AI, it does hinder the generalizability of the study. An appropriate next step would be to externally validate the model on a geographically distinct cohort prior to performing a validation study on a prospective cohort. Perhaps the greatest limitation of our study is the use of a clinically oriented definition of successful closure due to the lack of consistent post-treatment echocardiograms during our enrollment period. The only way to definitively determine if the PDA has closed is through echocardiography. As such, our clinical definition is prone to bias as the need for further treatment can vary between clinicians without sonographic confirmation. While this is a limitation, it does reflect the greater sense of ambivalence surrounding treatment of the PDA. Even if a PDA was still anatomically patent post-treatment echocardiogram, but the infant is no longer symptomatic then a clinician may deem treatment successful and not elect for further intervention. Therefore, although not ideal, the use of the clinical definition remains pertinent to the real-world management of the infant. Other limitations of our study include data quality and consistency. As noted in Table 1, there was significant inconsistency in the number and type of views present in our cohort. This is manifested in the variable performance of our model across domain types (Table 4). Furthermore, the secondary analysis summarized in Supplemental Table 5 shows that the model performance is related to quality of echocardiogram study. This suggests that if our imaging substrate was more standardized and of higher quality, our model may perform better. However, it is often a challenge to obtain high quality studies when assessing the PDA as the neonates are often critically ill and extremely premature, as was the case in our study. As such, perhaps a model such as ours that works well despite variable study quality is more clinically relevant than a better performing model that requires more standardized studies. Although interpretability is a common critique of all deep learning methodologies, the multimodal nature of our model does account for this limitation as several of the clinical factors incorporated have been demonstrated to be predictive of pharmacologic closure in previous studies with traditional methodologies (36). However, there remains the question of what exactly the model is identifying in the echocardiograms to help make its prediction. To better understand this question, we did generate saliency maps (Figure 3). While not fully explainable, these maps show that the logic of the CNN is consistent with the expected anatomic findings on echocardiogram. Despite these inherent challenges, however, the results of our investigation remain significant due to its innovative methodology and its potential to impact the approach to PDA in neonatal intensive care.

## Conclusion

In this retrospective study, we trained and internally validated a novel 3D computer vision model that successfully predicts the likelihood of successful pharmacologic closure of the PDA in preterm infants. The model, which is trained on pre-treatment echocardiogram and a set of clinical variables, is the first attempt to use deep learning to model treatment response. While effective in its task, the development of this model highlighted some challenges around the use of neonatal echocardiograms in computer vision models and more broadly limitations with interpretability in clinical AI. Nonetheless, the results of this study represent an important step in the management of the PDA and use of AI in clinical practice.
